title: Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis

cards.b: Two rival states shaped the Deccan for two centuries. UPSC asks about Krishnadevaraya, Hampi’s architecture, the Bahmani administration and the battle of Talikota.

Founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty on the Tungabhadra, with the sage Vidyaranya’s support. Four dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu. Capital Hampi. It was the “bulwark” of Hindu South against the north.

Tuluva dynasty’s greatest king. Defeated Orissa’s Gajapati and Bijapur; built Hazara Rama and Vittala temples; the Ashtadiggajas (eight poets) at court; wrote Amuktamalyada (Telugu). Visitors: Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz (Portuguese) praised Hampi. Allowed Portuguese trade and horses.

Kings with the mahamandaleswara and nayaks. Nayankara system: military chiefs held land and supplied troops. Ayagar system in villages (twelve officials). Revenue from land and trade. Seaborne trade: horses from Arabia, cloth and spices exported; ports Bhatkal, Mangalore. Temple endowments and irrigation (tanks and canals). Gold coin, the varaha or pagoda.

Founded in 1347 by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah in rebellion against Muhammad bin Tughlaq; capital Gulbarga, later Bidar. Muhammad Gawan, prime minister under Muhammad III, reorganised provinces (tarafs), the army and revenue; the Madrasa at Bidar; he was executed in 1481 (nobles’ rivalry: Deccanis vs Afaqis). Broke up into five: Bijapur (Adil Shah), Golconda (Qutb Shah), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shah), Berar (Imad Shah), Bidar (Barid Shah) by about 1518.

The combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeated Vijayanagara’s Rama Raya at Rakshasa-Tangadi (Talikota), 1565. Hampi was sacked for months. The empire survived in a smaller form under the Aravidu dynasty at Penukonda and Chandragiri until the 17th century. Reasons: Rama Raya’s overreach in Deccan politics, betrayal by Muslim generals in his army, and the alliance.

Vijayanagara: Hampi (UNESCO, 1986), Vittala temple with the stone chariot, Virupaksha temple, Lotus Mahal (Indo-Islamic). Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit flourished. Bahmani-Deccani: Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur), Golconda Fort, Charminar (Hyderabad, 1591), Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan (Bidar). Dakhni Urdu literature and Deccani painting. Mixed culture both ways.

Nineteenth-century writers (Robert Sewell, A Forgotten Empire, 1900) framed it as a Hindu resistance. Later historians (Burton Stein, Phillip Wagoner) note Persianate court dress and titles (“Hindu Sultan”, Hindu Suratrana) and shared military practice. Richard Eaton (A Social History of the Deccan) stresses cultural exchange.

Hampi is a living site with tourists and temple festivals; its stone chariot appears on the Rs 50 note. The Karnataka–Telangana–Andhra identity draws on both states. Water management at Hampi inspires modern tank restoration. The UNESCO status requires balance between tourism and conservation.
